pos: n. (the midland county of Coventry, where seven Lollards were burned in 1520 for teaching their children the Creed and the Lord's Prayer in English)
etymology: From Warwick, Old English Waeringwicum, the dwellings by the weir; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Warwickshire is the midland county of the Avon, holding Warwick, Stratford and the great city of Coventry, which in the fifteenth century was among the largest towns in England. Coventry held a Lollard community for a century and a half, detected and punished repeatedly, and in 1520 Bishop Geoffrey Blyth of Coventry and Lichfield proceeded against a group of its tradespeople. Seven were burned in the Little Park in April of that year, among them Mistress Joan Smith; the charges recorded against them were that they possessed English books and that they had taught their children the Lord's Prayer, the Creed and the Ten Commandments in English rather than in Latin. Four more Coventry people were burned under Mary in 1555 and 1557, including Laurence Saunders. The city's famous cycle of mystery plays was suppressed in the fifteen-seventies. The dictionary records the 1520 burnings as the clearest statement any English court ever made of what the old church objected to, since the offence charged was catechising in the mother tongue, and marks that the thing objected to became within twenty years the law of the land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer; the Creed as a brief summary of articles of faith; the mother tongue as the native language; to train as to form by practice; and a commandment as a precept.
webster_full: CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a symbol; that which is believed.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of speech; hence, speech; language; the whole sum of words used by a nation.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach and form by practice; as to train up a child in the way he should go.
COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; an order or injunction given by authority; a precept of the decalogue.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; and great shall be the peace of thy children.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
corruption_summary: Midland county whose city of Coventry held a long Lollard community and where seven of its tradespeople were burned in 1520, the charge being that they taught their children the Creed and the Lord's Prayer in English.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the withholding of the catechism from the people in their own speech, and Coventry in 1520 is where it was stated in court. The charge was not denial of a doctrine; it was teaching the Lord's Prayer, the Creed and the Commandments to children in English. That is a confession of what the system was protecting, and the dictionary names it as the priestly monopoly of the rudiments. Scripture puts the instruction of children in the hands of their parents as a plain duty, and the marginal reading at Proverbs 22:6 is Catechise, so that the command to “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) is a command to do precisely the thing for which seven Coventry people were burned.

The second paragraph marks the irony and draws the lesson, because the dictionary holds that the vindication came quickly and ought to be remembered. Within twenty years the Great Bible stood in English parish churches by royal authority, and within thirty the Prayer Book catechism was being taught in English in every parish in the realm. Timothy is commended for having known the holy scriptures from childhood, that “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15), and the promise Isaiah makes is of direct teaching, “all thy children shall be taught of the LORD” (Isa 54:13). The duty is also a duty of memory, and this entry exists to discharge it: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). Coventry's mystery plays were suppressed fifty years after its catechists were burned, and the dictionary counts the plays the lesser loss.

pos: n. (the midland county whose cathedral city of Lichfield saw Edward Wightman burned in 1612, the last man executed for heresy in England)
etymology: From Stafford, Old English Staeford, the ford by the staithe or landing place; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Staffordshire is the midland county of the moorlands and the potteries, holding the cathedral city of Lichfield, which with Coventry formed one of the great medieval dioceses. In 1612 Edward Wightman, a Burton-upon-Trent cloth merchant, was tried before Bishop Richard Neile and burned in Lichfield market place; he was the last person in England to be executed for heresy. What he held was genuinely heretical and the dictionary does not disguise it: the indictment lists the errors of Arius, Ebion, Cerinthus, Valentinian, Manes, Photinus and the Anabaptists, and Wightman had denied the Trinity, denied that Christ was God and man in one person, and claimed to be the prophet of Elijah and the Holy Spirit. He was brought to the stake once, cried out something taken for a recantation, was pulled out, refused to sign, and was burned a few weeks later. Lichfield had earlier burned Joyce Lewes under Mary in 1557. The dictionary names Wightman's doctrine as a damnable heresy and names his burning as a crime, and holds that the two judgments do not qualify each other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion; to try as to examine and prove; a wolf as a fierce animal of the dog kind; privily as secretly; and damnable as deserving condemnation.
webster_full: HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to prove by a test; to subject to a trial, in order to determine the quality of a thing.
WOLF, n. An animal of the canine kind, fierce and voracious; in Scripture, a figure for a false teacher.
PRIVILY, adv. Privately; secretly; in a manner not to be seen or observed.
DAMNABLE, a. That may be damned or condemned; deserving damnation; pernicious.
scriptures: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
corruption_summary: Midland county whose cathedral city of Lichfield burned Edward Wightman of Burton in 1612 for denying the Trinity, the last execution for heresy in England.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Wightman's own, and the dictionary names it without softening. He denied the Trinity and denied the two natures in one person, which is to deny the Christ of the Scriptures and so the only possible salvation; the ancient names on his indictment, Arius, Photinus, Manes, are correctly applied. The church is commanded to make exactly this kind of judgment and to make it by a test: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jn 4:1). Peter foretells such men inside the church and does not minimise the outcome, speaking of teachers “who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1). Our Lord's warning is to beware, for they “come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15).

The second corruption is the court's, and the dictionary names it as a crime because the remedy Scripture gives for heresy is never the fire. Every instrument the New Testament appoints is ecclesiastical: trying the spirits, admonition, rejection, excommunication, warning the flock. Paul tells the elders at Miletus that “after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock” (Act 20:29) and arms them with watchfulness and the word of grace, not with the sheriff. Wightman should have been excommunicated and refuted; he was chained to a post and burned twice over, having been dragged out of the first fire half-dead and sent back when he would not sign. The dictionary records this as the last of its kind in England and holds that a Protestant bishop who burns an Arian has not defended the Trinity but disgraced it, and has conceded in practice the very principle the Reformation denied, that error may be answered with the magistrate's fire.
roots_summary: Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test or try; Greek hairesis (G139), a heresy or sect; Greek lukos (G3074), a wolf.
roots_lines: Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove, to examine; “try the spirits whether they are of God”, 1 John 4:1.

“even denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1) — Wightman's actual doctrine, named plainly.
“not sparing the flock” (Act 20:29) — watchfulness, not the sheriff, as the remedy.

pos: n. (the midland county holding Lutterworth, where Wycliffe was rector and died in 1384 and whose bones were burned and cast into the Swift in 1428)
etymology: From Leicester, Old English Ligera ceaster, the Roman town of the Ligore people; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Leicestershire is the midland county of the Soar and the Wreake, and it holds the small town of Lutterworth in its southern corner. John Wycliffe was presented to the rectory of Lutterworth in 1374 and held it until he died there on the last day of 1384, having been driven out of Oxford and having spent his last years directing the translation of the Scriptures into English and writing against transubstantiation, the papal supremacy and the endowment of the church. He was struck down in his own church at the elevation of the host and died three days later. The Council of Constance condemned him in 1415 and ordered his remains dug up and burned; the sentence was carried out at Lutterworth in 1428 by Bishop Fleming, and the ashes were thrown into the river Swift, which runs into the Avon, the Avon into the Severn and the Severn into the sea. Thomas Fuller afterwards made the observation that the ashes were thus dispersed over the whole world, as his doctrine now is. The dictionary records the exhumation as the most futile act in English religious history.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to exhume as to dig out of the earth; to translate as to render into another language; to diminish as to lessen; to abide as to continue; and void as empty.
webster_full: EXHUME, v.t. To dig out of the earth what has been buried; to disinter.
TRANSLATE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
DIMINISH, v.t. To lessen; to make less or smaller by any means; to reduce; to take away a part.
ABIDE, v.i. To rest or dwell; to tarry or stay; to continue permanently or in the same state.
VOID, a. Empty; vacant; not occupied with any visible matter; having no legal or binding force.
scriptures: For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
corruption_summary: Midland county holding Lutterworth, where Wycliffe was rector from 1374 until his death in 1384 and where his bones were dug up and burned in 1428 and the ashes cast into the Swift.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Council of Constance's sentence on a dead man, and the dictionary names it as the public confession of a church that had run out of arguments. Wycliffe had been answered in his lifetime only by deprivation and condemnation, never refuted; forty-four years after his burial a bishop was sent to dig him up, burn what was left and throw it in a river. That is not church discipline, which cannot reach the dead, and it is not theology. It is an attempt to unmake a thing already done, and Scripture's standing promise about the Word makes the attempt absurd in advance: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

The second paragraph names the doctrine Wycliffe was condemned for holding and the dictionary holds with him, which is the sufficiency and finality of the written Word against additions. He argued that Scripture is the law of Christ and that what the church has added, the papal supremacy, the sacrifice of the mass, the mendicant orders, the whole apparatus of merit, is addition and must go. The rule he appealed to is given twice in Scripture at either end of the canon. Moses states it, “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2), and John closes the Revelation with the same guard, “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18). The effect of such a word once it is loose is not administrative, and the men at Lutterworth with their spades were handling something Jeremiah had described: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). The Swift carried the ashes to the Avon and the Avon to the sea.

roots_lines: Hebrew yasaph (H3254) — to add, to increase, to do again; “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you”, Deuteronomy 4:2.

Greek epitithemi (G2007) — to lay upon, to add to; “If any man shall add unto these things”, Revelation 22:18.

“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — the exhumation of 1428 and its futility.
“like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces” (Jer 23:29) — what the spades were sent against.

pos: n. (the midland county whose Particular Baptist association sent out William Carey and founded the modern missionary movement in 1792)
etymology: From Northampton, Old English Hamtun, the home settlement, distinguished as north from the southern Hamtun; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Northamptonshire is the midland county of the Nene, and in the dictionary it is the county from which the modern missionary movement came. Its Particular Baptist churches were associated from 1764 and included Olney, Kettering, Northampton, Moulton and Arnesby. Three men in that association are the key. John Sutcliff of Olney brought in from 1784 a monthly concert of prayer for the spread of the Gospel; Andrew Fuller of Kettering published The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation in 1785, breaking the hyper-Calvinist position that an unconverted man should not be called to believe; and William Carey, a shoemaker and then pastor at Moulton and Leicester, published An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians in 1792 and preached at Nottingham in May of that year on Isaiah 54, urging the brethren to expect great things and attempt great things. On the second of October 1792, in Martha Wallis's back parlour at Kettering, twelve ministers subscribed thirteen pounds two shillings and sixpence and formed the Particular Baptist Society for Propagating the Gospel among the Heathen. Carey sailed for Bengal the next year. The dictionary records that a world mission began in a parlour, among poor men, on a corrected doctrine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending; the heathen as the nations ignorant of the true God; an association as a body of churches united; an obligation as a binding duty; and to send as to despatch on an errand.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending; the act of sending; persons sent; a station of missionaries.
HEATHEN, n. A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
ASSOCIATION, n. The act of associating; union; connection; a society formed for transacting business in concert.
OBLIGATION, n. The binding power of a vow, promise, oath or contract; that which constitutes legal or moral duty.
SEND, v.t. To cause to go or pass from one place to another; to despatch on an errand or business.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
Isa 6:8
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
corruption_summary: Midland county whose Particular Baptist association, through Sutcliff's prayer call, Fuller's Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation and Carey's Enquiry, formed the first modern missionary society at Kettering in October 1792.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is hyper-Calvinism, and the dictionary names it precisely because it was an error of our own side and had to be answered from within. The high men of the eighteenth-century English Baptist churches held that since faith is a gift of God, no minister may address a general call to repent and believe to men who show no evidence of grace; the practical effect was pulpits that described the gospel and invited nobody, and a complete paralysis of mission. Fuller's answer, published at Kettering in 1785, was that the gospel is worthy of all acceptation and that it is every man's duty to believe it, and that the sovereignty of God in election is the reason mission will succeed rather than the reason not to attempt it. The commission admits no such restriction: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19).

The second paragraph names what replaced the error, which was a doctrine of the Father's promise to the Son. Carey and Fuller were not Arminians who had discovered zeal; they were Calvinists who had remembered that election guarantees a harvest. The ground of the whole enterprise is a grant already made: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). Where that is believed, the only question left is who goes, and the answer is a volunteer's: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me” (Isa 6:8). Carey, a shoemaker who had taught himself languages over his last, went; and the necessity he went under is the one Paul describes, “necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!” (1Co 9:16). Thirteen pounds and twelve poor ministers in a back parlour is the dictionary's favourite answer to the idea that doctrine does not matter practically.

“I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance” (Psa 2:8) — election as the ground of mission.
“Here am I; send me” (Isa 6:8) — Carey sailing for Bengal in 1793.

pos: n. (the smallest English county, whose motto claims much in little and whose Lyddington Bede House turned a bishop's palace into an almshouse)
etymology: Old English probably Roteland, Rota's land, or the red land from the ironstone soil; the county is first named in the eleventh century.
biblical_def: Rutland is the smallest county in England, some seventeen miles across at its widest, with Oakham and Uppingham as its two market towns and the motto Multum in Parvo, much in little. Its chief monument for the dictionary's purposes is at Lyddington, where the bishops of Lincoln had a palace; after the Reformation it passed to the Cecils, and in 1602 Thomas Cecil converted the great chamber and its range into the Bede House, an almshouse for twelve poor men and two women of the parish, which it remained for three centuries. Oakham and Uppingham both have schools founded in 1584 by Robert Johnson, archdeacon of Leicester, who also endowed hospitals in both towns. The county had few gentry, no city, no cathedral and almost no industry, and it produced no famous divine. The dictionary enters it deliberately, as the corpus has entered many great places, because the Scriptures are emphatic about the smallness of the instruments God uses, and because a palace turned into an almshouse for twelve poor men is a better use of a building than most dioceses ever managed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bede house as an almshouse; little as small in size or quantity; a flock as a company of sheep; strait as narrow; and to despise as to contemn.
webster_full: BEDE HOUSE, n. An almshouse; a house where poor persons pray for their benefactor; from bede, a prayer.
LITTLE, a. Small in size or extent; not great or large; of small dignity, power or importance.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation.
STRAIT, a. Narrow; close; not broad; confined; difficult; distressful.
DESPISE, v.t. To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of.
scriptures: Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Mat 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
corruption_summary: Smallest English county, with two market towns, no cathedral and no famous divine, whose Lyddington Bede House turned a bishop's palace into an almshouse for twelve poor men in 1602.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the scale on which God works is habitually small and that this is a doctrine rather than a consolation. Rutland has no cathedral, produced no divine whose name is remembered, and has been proposed for abolition more than once; it is in the dictionary because Scripture makes a point of rebuking the instinct that measures by size. Zechariah puts the rebuke as a question to men watching a poor remnant rebuild a temple that would not match the first: “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). The answer, generally, is everybody.

The second thing to recover is that the smallness extends to the number saved, and that our Lord says so without apology. The road is described as narrow and the travellers as few: “strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Mat 7:14). He names His own people with the same diminutive and attaches the largest possible promise to it, “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luk 12:32). And Isaiah states what the alternative to a remnant would have been, which settles the question of whether a small number is a failure: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9). Twelve poor men and two women housed in a bishop's great chamber at Lyddington for three hundred years is the kind of arithmetic the dictionary is content to record, and Robert Johnson's two schools and two hospitals in a county of this size are worth more than many a see.

pos: n. (the Worcestershire carpet town where Richard Baxter ministered from 1641 to 1660 and catechised eight hundred families house by house)
etymology: Old English Chideminstre, the minster or church of Cydda; the town later famous for its carpet weaving.
biblical_def: Kidderminster is the Worcestershire town on the Stour, and it is the most instructive parish in English pastoral history. Richard Baxter came as lecturer in 1641 to a town he described as ignorant, rude and reviling, with a drunken curate and a people who scarcely knew the catechism; apart from the war years he stayed until 1660. His method was deliberate and he published it. He preached twice on the Lord's day and once in the week; he and his assistant spent two whole days every week in private catechising, taking the families of the parish in turn, an hour to a family, going through the catechism and then applying it personally to each member; in this way the eight hundred families of the parish came round once a year. He found a church where the galleries had to be built to hold the hearers. Out of the experience came The Reformed Pastor in 1656, written for a ministers' meeting and the sharpest book on the ministry in English. Baxter's own doctrine of justification was faulty and the dictionary says so; his pastoral method it commends without reservation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister having the care of a church; to catechise as to instruct by question and answer; the counsel of God as his revealed purpose; to shun as to avoid; and sincerity as freedom from hypocrisy.
webster_full: PASTOR, n. A shepherd; one that has the care of flocks and herds; a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church.
CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to instruct in the principles of religion.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; deliberation; in theology, the revealed purpose and will of God.
SHUN, v.t. To avoid; to keep clear of; to refuse to meet or encounter; to neglect.
SINCERITY, n. Honesty of mind or intention; freedom from simulation or hypocrisy; purity of purpose.
scriptures: And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: Worcestershire town where Richard Baxter ministered from 1641 to 1660, catechising the parish's eight hundred families house by house two days a week, and out of which The Reformed Pastor came in 1656.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching from a pulpit is only half the pastoral office and that the other half is conducted at kitchen tables. Baxter's discovery at Kidderminster, which he pressed on every minister he could reach, was that he had preached for years to people who could not have stated the first article of the faith, and that an hour's private examination did more for a family than a year of sermons heard at a distance. Paul claims to have done both at Ephesus and names the second explicitly: “have taught you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20). He also claims completeness, that “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27), which is a standard a man can only know he has met if he has gone through the whole of it with people one by one.

The second thing to recover is that the method binds the minister before it binds the people. Baxter put himself and his assistant under two full days of catechising a week for the sake of eight hundred families, and he wrote The Reformed Pastor to tell other ministers that they were not doing their work. Paul's charge joins the man and the doctrine in one clause and makes the pastor's own soul part of the business: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee” (1Ti 4:16). The manner is to be open, with nothing managed and nothing held back, for the apostle renounced “the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2). The dictionary records that Baxter's own account of justification, with its place for faith and evangelical obedience as a personal righteousness, is an error that his admirers must not take with the method; and that the method, taken by itself, has never been bettered in England.

pos: n. (the Staffordshire town that was the royal seat of Mercia under Offa and sank to a market town after the Danes destroyed it)
etymology: Old English Tamanweorþig, the enclosure on the river Tame; weorþig meaning an enclosed settlement.
biblical_def: Tamworth stands where the Anker joins the Tame on the Staffordshire and Warwickshire border, and in the eighth century it was the principal residence of the kings of Mercia. Offa, who ruled from 757 to 796 and styled himself king of the whole land of the English, held his court and issued his charters there; Mercia was then the first power in Britain, with a bishopric raised at Lichfield to an archbishopric in 787 to free it from Canterbury. The Danes destroyed the place in 874, and though Aethelflaed of Mercia refortified it in 913 it never recovered its standing; the archbishopric had already been given up in 803. The collegiate church of St Editha was rebuilt after a fire in 1345. By the seventeenth century Tamworth was an ordinary market town, and it is chiefly remembered now for Peel's election address of 1834. The dictionary records the town as a case of a capital and an archbishopric both lost, and takes from it the plainest warning Scripture gives to those who reckon their security from their present eminence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a metropolitan as an archbishop; ease as rest or quiet; to remove as to displace; a candlestick as a holder for a candle; and eminence as a rising ground or distinction.
webster_full: METROPOLITAN, n. A bishop who presides over the other bishops of a province; an archbishop.
EASE, n. Rest; an undisturbed state; freedom from pain, disturbance or anxiety; quiet.
REMOVE, v.t. To cause to change place; to put from its place in any manner; to displace.
CANDLESTICK, n. An instrument or utensil to hold a candle, in which case it is a frame with a socket.
EMINENCE, n. Elevation; a rising ground; a hill of moderate elevation; exaltation in rank or station.
scriptures: Amo 6:1
Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Lam 2:9
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
corruption_summary: Staffordshire town that was Offa's royal seat and the centre of Mercian power, with an archbishopric at Lichfield from 787, reduced by the Danes in 874 to an ordinary market town.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the pursuit of ecclesiastical rank for political convenience, and Lichfield's archbishopric is the English textbook case. Offa wanted a metropolitan of his own rather than a Kentish one, and in 787 he got the pope to raise Lichfield to an archbishopric and divide the southern province; sixteen years after his death it was quietly abolished. A see created to suit a king's frontier is not an office of Christ's appointment but a department of state, and the dictionary names the whole transaction as the subordination of church order to national interest. Jeremiah states the general rule it broke: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD” (Jer 17:5).

The second paragraph takes the town's fate as a warning and applies it where Scripture applies it, to the comfortable. Amos addresses men secure in a capital and names their security as the problem: “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations” (Amo 6:1). The risen Christ makes the same point to a church rather than a kingdom, and makes it a matter of removal: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place” (Rev 2:5). Lamentations describes what such a removal looks like from inside, when the gates are sunk into the ground and “her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more” (Lam 2:9). A royal town that lost a court, an archbishopric and its walls within forty years is a short lesson in the subject, and the dictionary enters it for that reason rather than for Peel.

pos: n. (the Nottinghamshire market town within Sherwood Forest, long subject to forest law and later surrounded by the enclosures of the Dukeries)
etymology: Old English Mamesfeld, the open land by the hill called Mam; feld meaning open country rather than a field.
biblical_def: Mansfield is the Nottinghamshire market town lying in what was the heart of Sherwood Forest, and for most of its history it was governed by forest law. A royal forest was not woodland but a jurisdiction: the king's deer were protected across whole districts, the inhabitants could not fence, clear, hunt or in some cases even carry a bow, and a separate set of courts, the eyre and the swanimote, enforced it with heavy penalties against men whose living depended on the ground. Mansfield had a royal manor and was the administrative centre for the forest's southern part. From the sixteenth century onward the forest was progressively disafforested, and the great estates afterwards called the Dukeries, Welbeck, Clumber, Thoresby and Rufford, were carved out of it and enclosed; the commoners of the district lost grazing and fuel rights in the process, and in the nineteenth century the coal beneath it all made the owners richer still. The dictionary records Mansfield as a place to state the biblical law of property, which secures a poor man's inheritance against a powerful neighbour, and which both forest law and enclosure set aside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a forest as a tract reserved for the king's hunting; to enclose as to shut in with a fence; an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; common as belonging to many; and a reproach as censure.
webster_full: FOREST, n. An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees; in England, a royal forest reserved for the king's hunting.
ENCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut in; to fence or hedge about; to separate from common ground.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.
COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; public; general.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; the cause of shame or disgrace.
scriptures: And Naboth said to Ahab, The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.
Ecc 5:9
Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Nottinghamshire market town at the heart of Sherwood Forest, governed by forest law and its separate courts, and later ringed by the enclosed estates of the Dukeries carved out of the disafforested land.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the absorption of a poor man's rights into a great man's pleasure, and Mansfield suffered it twice, first under the forest and then under the enclosures. Scripture's set case on the subject is Naboth's, and the dictionary insists on how little it turns on price. Ahab offered money; Naboth answered that the land was not for sale on any terms: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). The inheritance of a family was held under God and not at the disposal of a king who wanted a garden, and Ahab's subsequent procurement of it by a legal process, two false witnesses and a judicial murder, is the precise shape of the thing the dictionary objects to in a private enclosure act.

The second paragraph sets out the principle on the other side, because the dictionary is not making a case against property. Property is assumed throughout Scripture and so is rank; what is forbidden is the use of rank to consume the property of the weak. Solomon states the dependence of every great man upon common labour, that “the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field” (Ecc 5:9), which places a duke and a commoner in one economy. The health of a nation is measured by its righteousness rather than its rent-rolls, since “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). And the whole requirement upon a man with power over his neighbours is stated in a sentence that leaves no room for the forest courts: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The coal found under the Dukeries made the owners richer and the commoners no better off, and the dictionary names that outcome as the ordinary fruit of the arrangement rather than a misfortune.

pos: n. (the Lincolnshire town whose dispute of 1627 over moving the communion table altarwise produced the classic Reformed English defence of the holy table)
etymology: Old English probably Granta ham, the homestead on the Granta or gravelly stream; a Lincolnshire market town on the Witham.
biblical_def: Grantham is the Lincolnshire market town on the Witham, with a parish church whose spire is among the tallest in England and a grammar school where Isaac Newton was a pupil. Its place in the dictionary is a parish quarrel that became a national argument. In 1627 the vicar, Peter Titley, moved the communion table from the body of the chancel, where it had stood table-wise since the Reformation with the people gathered round it, and set it altarwise against the east wall; the alderman and the townsmen objected and the matter went to the bishop of Lincoln, John Williams. Williams ruled for the townsmen, and in 1637 published his judgment and its grounds as The Holy Table, Name and Thing, arguing that the Church of England had deliberately replaced an altar with a table because it had replaced a sacrifice with a supper, and that to move the furniture back was to reintroduce by stealth the thing the Articles denied. Laud had him prosecuted in Star Chamber and imprisoned in the Tower. The dictionary records the case as the clearest English statement that furniture teaches doctrine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an altar as a place for sacrifice; a table as a board for meals; a supper as the evening meal; decently as in a becoming manner; and a tradition as a practice handed down.
webster_full: ALTAR, n. A mount, table or elevated place, on which sacrifices were anciently offered to some deity.
TABLE, n. An article of furniture consisting of a flat surface supported by legs; the table of the Lord's supper.
SUPPER, n. The evening meal; the last meal of the day; the Lord's supper, the sacrament of the eucharist.
DECENTLY, adv. In a decent or becoming manner; with propriety of behaviour; without immodesty.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices or rites from father to son by oral communication.
scriptures: Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
corruption_summary: Lincolnshire town whose vicar moved the communion table altarwise in 1627, against which Bishop John Williams ruled for the townsmen and published The Holy Table, Name and Thing in 1637, for which Laud imprisoned him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the restoration of the altar, and the dictionary names it as doctrine carried by carpentry. The Reformers had taken down stone altars and set up wooden tables in the body of the chancel because an altar implies a sacrifice and a priest who offers it, while a table implies a meal and guests who receive it; the change was deliberate and was the visible form of the Articles' denial that the mass is a propitiatory sacrifice. To push the table back against the east wall, rail it in and bow toward it was to teach the old doctrine again without having to argue it, which is why Williams fought over a few feet of chancel. Our Lord's rule removes the question from the realm of fittings altogether: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24).

The second paragraph grants the Laudian case its one real point and then answers it. Order in worship is commanded, and Paul closes his treatment of a disorderly church with the rule, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40); a parish where the table is set anywhere and treated anyhow is not thereby more spiritual. But order is not the same as ceremony, and an arrangement introduced by authority without warrant from Scripture falls under the Lord's own condemnation of worship that rests on human command: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). Paul describes the whole class of such observances as impressive and empty, having “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23). The dictionary adds that Williams was no Puritan, being a prelate who defended his own order; that he was imprisoned in the Tower for publishing a defence of the English Reformation's own settled practice is the measure of how far the Laudian party had travelled.

pos: n. (the Lincolnshire stone town of five parish churches, whose Browne's Hospital almshouse of 1475 survived the Reformation and still stands)
etymology: Old English Stanford, the stony ford, where the Great North Road crossed the Welland.
biblical_def: Stamford is the Lincolnshire town where the Great North Road crosses the Welland, built throughout of the local limestone, and one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. In the Middle Ages it had fourteen parish churches, five of which survive, four friaries, a Benedictine nunnery and for a brief period in 1333 a breakaway university of seceding Oxford scholars, suppressed by royal writ. Its most instructive survival is Browne's Hospital, founded about 1475 by William Browne, a wool merchant of the Calais staple, as an almshouse for ten poor men and two women with a warden and a confrater; it has a chapel and an audit room and medieval glass, and it has housed poor people continuously for five and a half centuries. Chantries and friaries went at the Reformation; the almshouse, being a charity for the living rather than an endowment for masses for the dead, was kept, reorganised and continued. The dictionary records the distinction as the sharpest practical test of the two religions, since the same merchant's money paid for both, and only one half of it was worth preserving.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an almshouse as a house for the poor; a chantry as an endowment for masses; mercy as tenderness shewn to an offender or sufferer; a warden as a keeper; and afflicted as grieved or distressed.
webster_full: ALMSHOUSE, n. A house appropriated for the use of the poor; a house maintained by charity.
CHANTRY, n. A church or chapel endowed with lands for the maintenance of priests to sing mass for the souls of the donors.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
WARDEN, n. A keeper; a guardian; one who has the care or superintendence of a house or institution.
AFFLICTED, a. Affected with continued or often repeated pain; greatly distressed; grieved.
scriptures: Hos 6:6
For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
Zep 3:12
I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD.
Jam 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
corruption_summary: Lincolnshire stone town of the Danelaw with five surviving parish churches, whose Browne's Hospital of about 1475 has housed poor people continuously while its chantries and friaries went at the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the chantry again, and Stamford is where the comparison can be made inside one man's will. William Browne, a wool merchant, spent his money on two things: masses for his soul and a house for twelve poor people. The first was swept away at the Reformation and the dictionary counts it a clean gain, since a purchased mass denies the completeness of Christ's one sacrifice and makes the relief of a dead man's estate a matter of coin. The second was kept and has run for five and a half centuries. Hosea states the preference that decides between them in a line: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos 6:6).

The second paragraph guards the judgment from a misuse, because the dictionary is not reducing religion to charity. Our Lord's rebuke to men who tithed herbs and omitted “the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Mat 23:23) is notable for adding that the lesser things ought also to have been done; he is correcting a proportion, not abolishing a duty. What the almshouse witnesses to is the kind of people God has said He will have about Him, “an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:12), and the kind of giver He accepts, since “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6). Fourteen parish churches in one small town is a monument to a religion of multiplied observance; five of them still standing and one almshouse still inhabited is a fair account of what survived the sifting, and the dictionary records that the sifting was done by the right criterion.
